correctness.rationale: For n≥2 and q,t in (0,1), with all predictions p_i=q, the treat-all decision is chosen iff q≥t. On A_n={1≤S_n≤n−1}, the observed relative utility is zero exactly when S_n/n≥t in the treat-all branch and S_n/n≤t in the treat-none branch. Summing the Bin(n,q) law, divided by P(A_n)=1−q^n−(1−q)^n, yields both exact integer-bounded tail formulas, including equality conventions. Independently recomputed exact rational cases against the original benchmark net-benefit definition; all matched. For fixed q≠t, standard binomial Chernoff/Stirling estimates give exception exponent D(t||q); at q=t, binomial CLT yields 1/2, and for q_n=t+c/√n a triangular-array CLT gives Φ(|c|/√(t(1−t))). Endpoint exclusion has vanishing probability at the limiting regimes. The checks are diagnostics, not the proof of asymptotics.
residual_risks: The conditional z_n is undefined when n=1 because P(A_n)=0; theorem is read for n≥2. The result assumes iid outcomes and perfectly constant known risk.

value.rationale: The source phenomenon is a specifically motivated risk-prediction interpretability issue, not an arbitrary probability exercise: perfectly calibrated constant predictions may receive zero observed utility with very high probability. The exact finite-sample conditional probability and the sharp threshold-local crossover quantify the sample sizes and risk/threshold separations at which the paradox appears. This is a natural, independently usable exact diagnostic invariant despite the standard binomial techniques and narrow iid model.
residual_risks: Algebra is elementary after the model reduction; results do not extend to heterogeneous, estimated or dependent risks.
